interviewQuestions.question: How would you tune a Dynamo-style store for read-heavy traffic?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the N/W/R relationship: I want reads fast since they dominate, so I'd keep R low — R=1 if I can tolerate it. To preserve the overlap guarantee (W+R>N), that means pushing W higher to compensate, so writes absorb more of the durability cost since they're the rarer operation.

Concretely, with N=3, I'd pick W=3, R=1: every write must reach all three replicas, but any single replica answers a read instantly. I'd only relax this (say to W=2) if I could tolerate writes occasionally failing when one replica is unreachable, trading a bit of write availability for the same R=1 read speed.

I'd also mention sloppy quorums as an escape hatch — if a replica is briefly unreachable, a hinted write to a different node keeps writes flowing without blocking on that node's recovery.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about the N/W/R trade-off concretely instead of reciting the formula.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Tuning quorums for read-heavy traffic

interviewQuestions.question: Explain what W+R>N actually guarantees, and what it doesn't.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start with what it guarantees: with N total replicas, if the write quorum size W and read quorum size R sum to more than N, any set of W replicas and any set of R replicas must share at least one replica — a pigeonhole argument, not a probabilistic one. That shared replica holds the most recent write, so a read that checks all R responses and takes the newest is guaranteed to see it.

What it doesn't guarantee: this assumes a strict quorum against the *correct* assigned replicas. If the system falls back to a sloppy quorum during a partition — writing to whichever nodes are reachable instead of the assigned ones — the overlap guarantee can be violated until hinted handoff completes. It also says nothing about concurrent writes to the same key; two clients writing at once can still race, and the system needs a separate mechanism (vector clocks, last-write-wins) to resolve that.

**Testing:** whether you can state the guarantee precisely and name its actual boundaries, not just recite the inequality.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What W+R>N guarantees and doesn't

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between a strict quorum and a sloppy quorum, and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd explain a strict quorum as requiring W or R to be satisfied specifically by the replicas assigned to that piece of data — if too many of them are down, the operation fails, full stop. A sloppy quorum relaxes that: if the assigned replicas aren't reachable, the write is temporarily accepted by any available node instead, which holds a hint pointing back to the node it actually belongs to, and hands the data off once that node recovers.

Why it matters: it's a direct availability-versus-correctness trade during a partition. Strict quorums keep the W+R>N consistency guarantee intact but sacrifice write availability when the "right" nodes are unreachable. Sloppy quorums keep accepting writes through the outage, but a read against only the assigned replicas can miss a hinted write until handoff finishes — the consistency guarantee has a real gap during that window.

**Testing:** whether you see sloppy quorums as a deliberate trade-off with a real consistency cost, not a free availability upgrade.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Strict vs sloppy quorums
